description: We are a team interested in the intersection of satellite technology, artificial intelligence, data science, and global finance. Our goal is to develop an interactive platform that uses NASA-ISRO's NISAR satellite data to detect environmental and physical changes worldwide and translate them into actionable intelligence.
summary:
Veyra is a satellite-monitoring platform that detects changes on Earth's surface and transforms complex satellite data into understandable, actionable information. It combines four layers: wide-area detection using NASA's NISAR radar; detailed investigation using LiDAR and high-resolution imagery; independent verification using additional satellite sources; and AI-powered explanations and alerts.

Veyra addresses the challenge of making complicated remote-sensing data accessible and reliable. It can identify changes associated with natural disasters, environmental damage, infrastructure, and observable military-related activity using publicly available satellite data. By comparing observations across different dates and sources, it helps distinguish unusual changes from normal conditions. Users can explore findings through interactive maps, 3D terrain visualizations, and before-and-after comparisons.

The platform integrates TigerData for data management and Twilio for SMS alerts. Across 207 trials, 185 passed and 22 failed. Veyra is important because it makes satellite intelligence more accessible, helping communities, researchers, and decision-makers better understand changes happening around the world.
details:
Veyra: Understanding What Changes on Earth

1. What Veyra Does

Veyra is a satellite-monitoring platform that detects changes on Earth's surface and explains them in plain English. It combines radar, LiDAR, high-resolution imagery, and environmental information to show what changed, where it happened, how reliable the evidence is, and why it may matter.

Unlike ordinary satellite photographs, radar can observe the ground through clouds, smoke, and darkness. Veyra turns these complicated observations into information that residents, researchers, emergency responders, farmers, and other users can understand.

2. Our Four-Layer Approach

Veyra uses four layers to turn satellite observations into useful information.

Layer 1 - Wide-Area Detection (NISAR)

Veyra uses NASA's NISAR satellite to scan large areas and identify unusual changes between observations. It compares images from the same viewing angle and checks whether the changes exceed normal background activity.

This allows Veyra to identify areas that deserve closer investigation, even when clouds or darkness prevent ordinary cameras from seeing the ground.

Layer 2 - Detailed Investigation (LiDAR and High-Resolution Imagery)

When NISAR identifies an area of interest, Veyra uses available LiDAR surveys to examine that location in greater detail.

Radar helps answer WHERE did something change? LiDAR helps answer HOW MUCH did it change?

LiDAR uses laser measurements to create detailed 3D maps. It can measure changes in elevation, terrain, buildings, and accumulated debris. Veyra can also use sharper commercial satellite imagery to provide additional visual detail where available.

Layer 3 - Independent Verification and Context

Before presenting an important finding, Veyra checks it against independent sources, including Europe's Sentinel-1 radar, previous satellite observations, LiDAR data, and environmental records.

It also filters out misleading results, such as flooded areas being mistaken for permanent terrain changes or underwater surfaces being mistaken for land damage.

The goal is to distinguish genuine changes from normal environmental activity and measurement errors.

Layer 4 - Intelligence, Insights, and Alerts

Veyra combines the verified observations with relevant information to explain what may have happened and why it matters.

Its AI translates measured results into simple explanations, while the scientific calculations remain separate from AI-generated text. The platform can then display findings on an interactive map, provide practical recommendations, and send SMS alerts through its integrated Twilio system.

3. Monitoring More Than Natural Disasters

Veyra is designed to examine different kinds of changes, including natural disasters, infrastructure, environmental activity, and large-scale military-related activity.

For example, when examining a military-related location, Veyra can compare publicly available satellite observations over time to identify changes in visible aircraft or vehicle presence, activity around facilities, and activity at ports or other infrastructure.

Radar can help detect changes even when clouds or darkness limit optical imagery. Higher-resolution imagery can provide additional visual context, while independent observations help establish whether a change is consistent across different sources.

This is intended for broad situational awareness and research. Satellite observations cannot establish military intentions, identify every object with certainty, or prove that an observed change represents a particular operation.

4. Real-World Examples

  • Upper Trishuli 3A, Nepal (August 2026): Veyra's analysis measured 0.59 km² of changed ground between August 19 and 31, compared with 0.15 km² during the earlier quiet period. Sentinel-1 showed changes in corresponding areas. The closest area of agreement was 61 meters from the hydropower plant.
  • Palisades Fire, California (January 2025): LiDAR comparisons identified 108,720 m² of lowered ground in a one-square-kilometer area, consistent with major changes to buildings and vegetation.
  • Eaton Fire Debris Basins, California (2025–2026): Repeat drone LiDAR surveys helped measure sediment entering debris basins. One December survey measured 9,924 m³ in the Lincoln basin.
  • Hurricane Ian, Florida (2022): LiDAR comparisons identified 35,700 m² of lowered ground around Fort Myers Beach.

These are project analysis results, not claims that satellite measurements alone establish the cause of every change.

5. Main Features

  • Interactive globe that transitions from NASA night-light data to detailed satellite imagery.
  • Before-and-after satellite comparisons and date-by-date observation history.
  • 3D LiDAR viewer showing terrain and elevation changes.
  • Independent verification panels showing how different data sources compare.
  • Environmental layers for fires, heat, rainfall, methane, surface water, and land disturbance.
  • Actionable Insights that help users understand potential impacts and practical next steps.
  • SMS notifications through Twilio.

6. Technology and Infrastructure

Veyra is built with Next.js, React, MapLibre, Three.js, and deck.gl. Its data-processing system uses Python tools including NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, h5py, pyproj, and laspy.

Its data sources include NASA NISAR, NASA environmental datasets, Europe's Sentinel satellites, and available LiDAR surveys from sources such as USGS, NOAA, and OpenTopography. Commercial imagery from providers such as Umbra, Capella, and ICEYE can provide additional detail where available.

TigerData is integrated to support Veyra's data storage and querying

Twilio will soon be integrated to deliver SMS alerts for people with limited internet access.

7. Limitations, Solutions, and Testing

Satellite monitoring has limitations. NISAR does not observe every location continuously, clouds can interfere with laser and optical surveys, and radar changes can sometimes be caused by ordinary environmental conditions rather than damage.

Veyra addresses these problems by:

  • Comparing observations from different dates and the same viewing angle.
  • Using Sentinel-1 as an independent radar check.
  • Using LiDAR for detailed measurements in areas identified for further investigation.
  • Filtering out misleading results involving water and other unreliable measurements.
  • Separating confirmed measurements from possible explanations.
  • Using additional imagery and environmental records to provide context.

Veyra has completed 207 trials, with 178 passing and 29 failing, an approximately 85.99% pass rate. The failed trials help identify weaknesses that can be corrected and tested again.

The goal is to make satellite monitoring more understandable, more reliable, and more useful to people who need to know what is changing around them.
